docs.title: cmenpy
docs.text: Compute Metaheuristic Engine for Python (cmenpy or /siːmɛnpaɪ/) is an extensible, flexible and vectorized Python framework for designing and prototyping metaheuristic and population-based optimization algorithms.

docs.title: Core pillars
docs.text:
• Vectorized data structures: population arrays, agent states and search spaces use a flattened, vectorized layout with no heavy per-individual objects, and interoperate natively with NumPy and Numba.
  • Extensible architecture: custom operators, mutation rules or whole new paradigms only require overriding a few decoupled methods.
  • Non-monolithic flexibility: no visualization tools, file exporters or rigid loggers — just the mathematical engine and its structural flow.
  • Research ready: licensed under GNU GPLv3.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install cmenpy          # runtime: numpy + numba only

For development (tests, type checks, docs):

uv sync --extra dev         # runtime + dev tools
uv sync --extra docs        # ... plus the MkDocs toolchain

Requires Python >=3.11.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text: Path Contents cmenpy/ The package. Public subpackages: compile (numba kernels), model (declaration styles), population (population handling), target (objectives), kernel (buffers), bounds (search space), context (the ctx object), functools (comparators). Internal support: epoch, generator, hints, tracker. tests/ Test suite mirroring the package (pytest) example/ Runnable algorithms and demos (not shipped in the wheel) docs/ This site (MkDocs + Material)

docs.title: Version 2026b0
docs.text:
• A decent and civilized version, compatible with GNU GPLv3
  • Numba decorators accept parameter annotations ("Array[float, 2]", "Scalar[float]", and mypy-clean Annotated[..., cm.Array[...]]), in addition to the positional cm.Array / cm.Scalar markers.
  • cm.jit is renamed to cm.precompile (both use numba.njit); cm.jit remains as a deprecated alias that emits a DeprecationWarning.
  • cm.precompile (and the cm.jit alias) expose the numba.njit options fastmath and parallel; other numba options are forwarded as keywords.
  • cm.vectorize and cm.reduce also accept fastmath=True and parallel=True (parallel maps to numba's target="parallel").
  • Decorators return a deferred _Kernel; kernels compile on first use (or via cm.prepare). A @cm.template model configures parallel, fastmath and cache at instantiation and they propagate to its kernels.
  • cm.parallel is removed; use cm.precompile(parallel=True) standalone, or a model instantiated with parallel=True for kernels marked parallel=True.
  • cm.guvectorize is renamed to cm.reduce (generalized ufunc). The layout is inferred from typed annotations (Array[float, 'm,n'], last parameter is the output); cm.Contract[[inputs...], output] remains as the explicit signature marker.

docs.title: Version 0.0.0
docs.text:
• Experimental test version
  • Modeled by decorators
  • Implementation of basic and primitive structure
  • Population vectorization to leverage SIMD

docs.title: Numba kernels
docs.text: cmenpy.compile exposes three decorators. Each returns a _Kernel descriptor that compiles lazily on first use (or eagerly via cm.prepare(model) / solve(..., prepare=True)) and auto-casts its arguments. nopython=True is always enabled.

docs.title: Declaring specs
docs.text:
Specs can be passed positionally (cm.Array[...] / cm.Scalar[...] markers: bare means untyped, e.g. cm.Array[float, 2] is float64 with rank 2) or as parameter annotations:

@cm.precompile
def hunt(X: "Array[float, 2]", a: "Scalar[float]"): ...

# mypy-clean form (identical meaning):
def hunt(X: typing.Annotated[npt.NDArray[np.float64], cm.Array[float, 2]]): ...

Plain (non-marker) hints are ignored; positional markers win over annotations.

docs.title: @cm.precompile (njit)
docs.text:
@cm.precompile(parallel=True)
def hunt(X: "Array[float, 2]", leaders: "Array[float, 2]"):
    out = np.empty_like(X)
    for i in nb.prange(X.shape[0]):
        ...
    return out

Maps to numba.njit. fastmath and parallel are first-class options (parallel also needs nb.prange in the body); any other numba option (cache=True, boundscheck=False, …) is forwarded as a keyword.

Deprecated / removed

cm.jit remains as a deprecated alias that emits a DeprecationWarning. The old @cm.parallel is gone — use @cm.precompile(parallel=True).

docs.title: @cm.vectorize (ufunc)
docs.text:
@cm.vectorize
def scale(r: "Scalar[float]", a: "Scalar[float]") -> "Scalar[float]":
    return a * (2.0 * r - 1.0)

Elementwise ufunc with automatic casting. A fully typed kernel needs a full signature: positionally cm.Scalar[float, [cm.Scalar[float], cm.Scalar[float]]] (return dtype first), or a typed return annotation. A partially typed @cm.vectorize raises TypeError. Accepts fastmath/parallel (parallel maps to numba's target="parallel").

docs.title: @cm.reduce (generalized ufunc)
docs.text:
The preferred form infers the layout from typed annotations — the last parameter is the output:

@cm.reduce
def matmul(a: "Array[float, 'm,n']", b: "Array[float, 'n,k']",
           out: "Array[float, 'm,k']"):
    ...
# layout (m,n),(n,k)->(m,k), outputs allocated by numba

The explicit cm.Contract[[inputs...], output] marker remains for full control:

@cm.reduce(cm.Contract[[float, float, ..., ..., ...], float]])
def combine(a, b, s1, s2, s3, out): ...   # (n),(n),(),(),()->(n)

Contract shorthand: a plain dtype is Array[dtype, "n"], ... is a default-float scalar, Array[dtype] is a whole-array argument with a private dimension, and Array[dtype, "m,n"] names its dimensions. The legacy (signatures, layout) pair is still accepted. Accepts fastmath=True and parallel=True (target="parallel").

docs.title: Model compile options
docs.text:
A @cm.template model sets options at instantiation and they propagate to every kernel — fastmath/cache apply when the model or the kernel asks, while parallel on a precompile kernel additionally requires the kernel to have opted in with parallel=True (it needs nb.prange):

model = GreyWolfOptimizer(seed=1, parallel=True, fastmath=True, cache=True)
model.prepare()              # force compilation, report signatures
cm.prepare(SomeClass)        # same for a standalone kernel holder

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
A model is an optimizer you describe once and then run against any objective. cmenpy offers two declaration styles that produce the same contract — a callable exposing:

(best_fitness, best_x) = model.solve(
    f, bounds, epochs, pop_size, pop_range=None, debug=False, sense="min"
)
  • @cm.declare wraps a function. Best when one function body drives the whole run and you want parameters bound by keyword.
  • @cm.template wraps a class. Best when you want per-instance state, an explicit initialize/evolve split, and numba kernels that inherit compile options.

Both yield a BaseOptimizer with .solve(...), .alias and .tracker.

docs.title: @cm.declare over a function
docs.text:
@cm.declare(x=cm.Argument[int, (0, 3), 2])
def algo(args, epoch, ctx):
    pop = cm.PopulationSwarm(ctx.buff)
    pop.compute << ctx.rng.uniform(ctx.bounds.low, ctx.bounds.up,
                                   (pop.size, ctx.bounds.ndim))
    for _ in epoch:
        ...  # one epoch of your operator

The decorated function receives three arguments:

Argument Meaning args The bound cm.Argument fields (read args.x) epoch An EpochIteration — iterate it, or read epoch.max ctx The run context (see below)

Parameters are declared as keyword cm.Argument fields and bound by calling the model first, which returns a ready-to-run optimizer:

model = algo(x=1)            # bind the declared field
best  = model.solve(f, bounds, epochs=150, pop_size=15)

Because the whole run lives inside one function, the loop is explicit: you iterate epoch yourself. This style mirrors a plain script and is the easiest starting point — see example/hello_world_v1.py.

docs.title: @cm.template over a class
docs.text:
@cm.template
class MyAlgorithm:
    a: cm.Argument[int, (1, 100)]   # tunable, range-checked
    w: cm.Variable[np.ndarray]      # free internal state

    def initialize(self, ctx) -> None:
        pop = cm.PopulationSwarm(ctx.buff)
        pop.compute << ctx.rng.uniform(-1, 1, (pop.size, ctx.bounds.ndim))

    def evolve(self, e, ctx) -> None:
        ...  # advance one epoch; called once per epoch

The lifecycle is fixed and driven by solve:

  • initialize(ctx) runs once, before any epoch — seed the population and set up state here.
  • evolve(e, ctx) runs once per epoch, with e the current epoch index.

Fields are declared as class annotations:

Marker Meaning cm.Argument[type] Required, no range/default cm.Argument[type, default] With a default value cm.Argument[type, (min, max)] Range-checked, required cm.Argument[type, (min, max), default] Range-checked, with default cm.Variable[type] Free internal state (no range, no default)

Bind fields (and the seed) via the constructor call, then solve:

model = MyAlgorithm(a=3, seed=1)
best  = model.solve(f, bounds, 150, 15)

The template style is the natural home for numba kernels: declare them as methods with @cm.precompile / @cm.vectorize / @cm.reduce, and they receive the model's compile options at instantiation — MyAlgorithm(seed=1, parallel=True, fastmath=True, cache=True) (see Numba kernels). See example/hello_world_v2.py and the optimizers in example/.

Choosing a style

Reach for @cm.declare for quick, script-like experiments and @cm.template for reusable optimizers with state, compiled kernels, or an initialize/evolve split. For a full walk-through, see Build a custom model.

docs.title: The ctx object
docs.text:
The context passed to initialize/evolve exposes:

Attribute Meaning ctx.buff The KernelBuffer backing the population ctx.bounds The search-space Bounds (low, up, ndim) ctx.rng The random generator ctx.sense "min" or "max" — propagate it instead of hard-coding ctx.epoch / ctx.epochs Current epoch / total ctx.target / ctx.f The wrapped objective

Note

Use ctx.sense (or the cm.is_best / cm.is_worst comparators, which take a sense) rather than hard-coding < or >, so your model works for both minimization and maximization.

docs.title: Introspection
docs.text:
A template model exposes a few useful hooks:

  • model.model_class — the wrapped class.
  • model.compile_options — the resolved parallel/fastmath/cache flags.
  • model.prepare() — force-compile all kernels and return their signatures.
  • model.tracker — the per-epoch history (populated when solve(..., debug=True)).

docs.title: API
docs.text: Autodoc for the model layer (decorators, markers, optimizers, protocols) lives in the API Reference → Models. To build your own model from scratch, follow Build a custom model.

docs.title: Population
docs.text:
cm.PopulationSwarm(buffer) is the main handle over a KernelBuffer — a (pop_size, ndim+1) store with fitness in column 0 and the solution vector from column 1.

pop = cm.PopulationSwarm(ctx.buff)     # pop.X = solutions, pop.F = fitness
pop.compute << values                  # write a whole (pop_size, ndim) block and score it
pop.assign[mask] << pop.access[mask]   # copy rows (access = read-only, assign = writable)
~pop.extract                           # active/found solutions; ~pop.idx / ~pop.F filter active rows
  • Iterate with for i in pop: or for i in ~pop:.
  • Selection and ranking follow ctx.sense ("min"/"max"): pop.best, pop.worst, pop.sort, plus cm.best_index / cm.worst_index and the cm.is_best((new_F, old_F), ctx.sense) comparator.
  • Manage the roster with pop.size, pop.insert(x), pop.remove(i), pop.free_space.
  • The usual offspring pattern scores candidates in a fresh buffer and merges: ctx.buff.snapshot → score → merge with cm.is_best.

docs.title: API
docs.text: Autodoc for the swarm handle, operators, matrix views and agents lives in the API Reference → Population. The buffer types are under Kernel, the comparators under Utilities, and Bounds under Bounds.

docs.title: Function style: @cm.declare
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import cmenpy as cm


@cm.declare(x=cm.Argument[int, (0, 3), 2])
def my_algorithm(args, epoch, ctx):
    pop = cm.PopulationSwarm(ctx.buff)
    pop.compute << ctx.rng.uniform(
        ctx.bounds.low, ctx.bounds.up, (pop.size, ctx.bounds.ndim)
    )
    # ... one epoch of your operator ...


best = my_algorithm(x=1).solve(
    lambda x: np.sum(x**2), cm.Bounds([(-1, 1)] * 3), epochs=150, pop_size=15
)

Full version: example/hello_world_v1.py.

docs.title: Class style: @cm.template
docs.text:
@cm.template
class MyAlgorithm:
    a: cm.Argument[int, (1, 100)]

    w: cm.Variable[np.array]

    def initialize(self, ctx) -> None:
        pop = cm.PopulationSwarm(ctx.buff)
        pop.compute << ctx.rng.uniform(-1, 1, (pop.size, ctx.bounds.ndim))

    def evolve(self, e, ctx) -> None:
        # ... generation `e` ...
        ...


model = MyAlgorithm(a=3, seed=1)
best = model.solve(lambda x: np.sum(x**2), cm.Bounds([(-1, 1)] * 3), 150, 15)

Full version: example/hello_world_v2.py.

docs.title: The solve contract
docs.text:
(best_fitness, best_x) = model.solve(
    f, bounds, epochs, pop_size, pop_range=None, debug=False, sense="min"
)
  • f is a callable x -> float over one solution vector (or a vectorized target).
  • bounds is a cm.Bounds (e.g. cm.Bounds([(-1, 1)] * ndim)).
  • sense is "min" (default) or "max".

docs.title: Run the examples
docs.text:
example/ is not a declared dependency target and is excluded from the wheel. Some examples import opfunu, which must be installed separately:

uv pip install opfunu
.venv/bin/python example/hello_world_v1.py
.venv/bin/python example/reduce_demo.py

See Examples for the full catalogue of runnable algorithms.

docs.title: Target functions
docs.text: A target is the objective you are optimizing. cmenpy wraps it in a TargetFunction that counts function evaluations (NFE) and enforces an optional budget, then scores the population every epoch.

docs.title: Evaluation modes
docs.text:
There are two ways a target is scored, and the difference is the single most important performance lever in cmenpy:

Mode How it scores When Row-by-row (default) np.apply_along_axis — one Python call per individual A plain callable Vectorized (fast) A single call over the whole (pop, ndim) block Wrapped with cm.vectorized_target

A plain Python callable works, but it pays a per-individual Python-call overhead:

def sphere(x):                     # x: one solution vector -> one float
    return float(np.sum(x**2))

model.solve(sphere, bounds, epochs, pop_size)     # scored row-by-row

A vectorized target receives the entire active block at once and returns one fitness per row, so the whole population is dispatched in one call:

import numpy as np

def sphere_block(X):               # X: (pop, ndim) -> (pop,)
    return np.sum(X**2, axis=1)

model.solve(cm.vectorized_target(sphere_block), bounds, epochs, pop_size)

docs.title: cm.vectorized_target
docs.text:
cm.vectorized_target(fn) marks fn as able to score a whole block, returning a VectorizedTarget. The contract is strict:

  • Input is a 2-D array of shape (pop, ndim).
  • Output is a 1-D array of length pop — one value per row.
  • The result is identical to row-by-row evaluation, only dispatched once.

The marker is checked with is True, so it must be exactly True on the wrapper. A truthy stand-in (e.g. vectorized = "yes") does not count and the target silently falls back to row-by-row. cm.vectorized_target is the only supported way to set it.

When to reach for it

Any objective with per-solution math (sums, products, norms, trig) vectorizes cleanly with NumPy broadcasting. If your objective is already written as (pop, ndim) -> (pop,), wrapping it is a near-free speedup — especially for large populations or expensive functions.

docs.title: Vectorize with Numba
docs.text:
For objectives heavy enough that NumPy still leaves time on the table, compile the block kernel with @cm.precompile (numba njit) and then wrap it in cm.vectorized_target. Two things must line up:

  1. The kernel takes the whole block — annotate it as Array[float, 2] and return a (pop,) array (e.g. with np.sum(..., axis=1)).
  2. Wrap the compiled kernel in cm.vectorized_target so cmenpy scores the block in one call instead of falling back to row-by-row.
import cmenpy as cm


@cm.precompile
def sphere_numba(X: "Array[float, 2]"):
    return np.sum(X**2, axis=1)          # (pop, ndim) -> (pop,)


best = model.solve(
    cm.vectorized_target(sphere_numba), bounds, epochs, pop_size
)

The kernel compiles on first evaluation and then reports its signature; wrap it in cm.vectorized_target so cmenpy dispatches the block in one call instead of falling back to row-by-row. The two pieces are complementary:

@cm.precompile          -> compile the block math with numba
cm.vectorized_target   -> tell cmenpy to dispatch the block in one call

cm.prepare is for models/classes

To force-compile the kernels declared on a model class, use model.prepare() / cm.prepare(SomeClass) (see Numba kernels). A standalone kernel like the one above instead compiles on first use and reports via .signatures().

Elementwise ufuncs

@cm.vectorize (a numba ufunc) is the tool for elementwise helpers, not whole-block objectives — it maps a scalar kernel over an array. For an objective you want the block form ((pop, ndim) -> (pop,)), prefer @cm.precompile as above. See Numba kernels for both.

docs.title: NFE budget
docs.text:
TargetFunction counts every evaluation and can stop the run early. Pass max_nfe to the wrapper; when the budget is spent it raises MaxNumberOfCalls:

from cmenpy.target import MaxNumberOfCalls, TargetFunction

tf = TargetFunction(sphere, bounds, max_nfe=10_000)
try:
    model.solve(tf, bounds, epochs, pop_size)
except MaxNumberOfCalls:
    ...

The running count is available as tf.nfe, and the sense-aware dispatch lives in KernelBuffer.apply (see Kernel).

docs.title: Choosing a target
docs.text:
• Prototyping — a plain callable is fine; start here.
  • Large populations / costly objectives — wrap a NumPy (pop, ndim) -> (pop,) function with cm.vectorized_target.
  • Hot inner loop — compile the block kernel with @cm.precompile and wrap it with cm.vectorized_target.
  • Strict evaluation budget — set max_nfe and catch MaxNumberOfCalls.

Runnable examples of each pattern are in example/ (see Examples).

docs.title: Build a custom model
docs.text:
This tutorial walks through implementing a custom optimizer from scratch with the @cm.template class style. We will build a (μ + λ) Evolution Strategy (Es): keep a parent population of size μ, produce λ offspring by Gaussian mutation each epoch, and select the best μ from the union of parents and offspring (elitist selection).

Along the way you will use every core piece of cmenpy: fields, the ctx object, the Population DSL, the comparators, and a compiled numba kernel.

Prerequisites

Comfortable with NumPy. You should have skimmed the Quickstart and Models overview.

docs.title: What we are building
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import cmenpy as cm

@cm.template
class EvolutionStrategy:
    sigma: cm.Argument[float, (1e-6, 10.0), 0.5]   # mutation step (initial)

    def initialize(self, ctx) -> None: ...
    def evolve(self, e, ctx) -> None: ...

model = EvolutionStrategy(seed=42)
best_fitness, best_x = model.solve(
    lambda x: np.sum(x**2), cm.Bounds([(-1, 1)] * 5), epochs=100, pop_size=30
)

Let's build it step by step.

docs.title: Step 1 — Declare the class and fields
docs.text:
Start with the skeleton. Class annotations declare tunable parameters with cm.Argument[type, (min, max), default] and free state with cm.Variable[type]:

@cm.template
class EvolutionStrategy:
    sigma: cm.Argument[float, (1e-6, 10.0), 0.5]

    offspring: cm.Variable[np.ndarray]
  • sigma is a tunable argument: range-checked, with a default, and settable at construction (EvolutionStrategy(sigma=0.1)).
  • offspring is a variable: internal state with no range or default. We will store the current generation's offspring here so evolve can both produce and score them.

A @cm.template model must implement two methods: initialize(self, ctx) (runs once) and evolve(self, e, ctx) (runs once per epoch). Let's add them next.

docs.title: Step 2 — Seed the population in initialize
docs.text:
initialize runs before any epoch. Build a PopulationSwarm over the buffer and write an initial random population with pop.compute << ..., which both inserts and scores the solutions:

def initialize(self, ctx) -> None:
    pop = cm.PopulationSwarm(ctx.buff)
    pop.compute << ctx.rng.uniform(
        ctx.bounds.low, ctx.bounds.up, (pop.size, ctx.bounds.ndim)
    )
  • ctx.buff is the flat buffer backing the population.
  • ctx.bounds.low / ctx.bounds.up are the box bounds — convenient for vectorized sampling.
  • pop.size is the number of active individuals.

After this line the whole parent population is randomly placed and evaluated.

docs.title: Step 3 — Produce offspring in evolve
docs.text:
evolve(self, e, ctx) is called once per epoch with the epoch index e. We mutate μ randomly chosen parents λ times. First, grab the active parent solutions (~pop.extract), then sample parent indices and perturb:

def evolve(self, e, ctx) -> None:
    pop = cm.PopulationSwarm(ctx.buff)
    parents = ~pop.extract                       # (μ, ndim) active solutions

    # Anneal the step size linearly over the run.
    self.offspring = self.sigma * (1.0 - e / ctx.epochs)

    idx = ctx.rng.integers(0, pop.size, pop.size)  # λ = μ
    kids = parents[idx]                            # pick parents at random

    noise = ctx.rng.standard_normal(kids.shape)
    mutated = np.clip(
        kids + self.offspring * noise,
        ctx.bounds.low,
        ctx.bounds.up,
    )

We reuse the buffer's snapshot to score the offspring in isolation, without clobbering the parents yet:

    n_pop = cm.PopulationSwarm(ctx.buff.snapshot)
    n_pop.compute << mutated

ctx.buff.snapshot

snapshot returns a fresh, empty buffer of the same shape wired to the same objective and sense. It is the idiomatic place to evaluate a candidate generation before merging it back.

docs.title: Step 4 — Elitist selection with cm.is_best
docs.text:
Now merge: keep, for each row, whichever of {parent, offspring} is better. The cm.is_best((new_F, old_F), ctx.sense) comparator returns the row indices where new beats old, respecting the optimization direction:

    mask = cm.is_best((n_pop.F, pop.F), ctx.sense)
    pop.assign[mask] << n_pop.access[mask]
  • n_pop.F / pop.F are the fitness columns of the offspring and parents.
  • pop.assign[mask] << n_pop.access[mask] copies the winning offspring rows over their parents (access reads whole rows, assign writes them).

Because we never introduce a worse individual, the best solution is monotonically non-worsening — classic elitism. Note we used ctx.sense rather than a hard-coded comparison, so this model works for "min" and "max" alike.

docs.title: Step 5 — Compile the mutation with a numba kernel
docs.text:
The mutation loop above is plain NumPy. To make it run at numba speed, move the per-gene math into a @cm.precompile kernel declared as a method. Annotate the parameters so cmenpy knows how to cast and type them:

@cm.template
class EvolutionStrategy:
    sigma: cm.Argument[float, (1e-6, 10.0), 0.5]
    offspring: cm.Variable[np.ndarray]

    @cm.precompile
    def mutate(
        K: "Array[float, 2]",
        N: "Array[float, 2]",
        s: "Scalar[float]",
        lo: "Scalar[float]",
        hi: "Scalar[float]",
    ):
        out = np.empty_like(K)
        for i in range(K.shape[0]):
            for j in range(K.shape[1]):
                v = K[i, j] + s * N[i, j]
                out[i, j] = min(max(v, lo), hi)   # clip to bounds
        return out

Then call it from evolve instead of the inline NumPy:

    mutated = self.mutate(kids, noise, self.offspring,
                          ctx.bounds.low, ctx.bounds.up)

Because mutate is a method on a @cm.template class, it participates in the model's compile options — you can force parallel, fastmath or cache at construction (see Numba kernels). The kernel compiles lazily on first use; call model.prepare() to compile eagerly and inspect the signatures.

docs.title: Step 6 — Run it
docs.text:
Wire it all together and solve:

if __name__ == "__main__":
    model = EvolutionStrategy(seed=42)

    def sphere(x):
        return float(np.sum(x**2))

    best_fitness, best_x = model.solve(
        sphere, cm.Bounds([(-1, 1)] * 5), epochs=100, pop_size=30
    )
    print("best fitness:", best_fitness)
    print("best solution:", best_x)

solve returns (best_fitness, best_x). Pass debug=True to populate model.tracker with per-epoch history (EpochHistory records), and sense="max" to switch to maximization.

docs.title: Full example
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import cmenpy as cm


@cm.template
class EvolutionStrategy:
    """A (mu + lambda) Evolution Strategy with elitist selection."""

    sigma: cm.Argument[float, (1e-6, 10.0), 0.5]

    offspring: cm.Variable[np.ndarray]

    @cm.precompile
    def mutate(
        K: "Array[float, 2]",
        N: "Array[float, 2]",
        s: "Scalar[float]",
        lo: "Scalar[float]",
        hi: "Scalar[float]",
    ):
        out = np.empty_like(K)
        for i in range(K.shape[0]):
            for j in range(K.shape[1]):
                v = K[i, j] + s * N[i, j]
                out[i, j] = min(max(v, lo), hi)
        return out

    def initialize(self, ctx) -> None:
        pop = cm.PopulationSwarm(ctx.buff)
        pop.compute << ctx.rng.uniform(
            ctx.bounds.low, ctx.bounds.up, (pop.size, ctx.bounds.ndim)
        )

    def evolve(self, e, ctx) -> None:
        pop = cm.PopulationSwarm(ctx.buff)
        parents = ~pop.extract

        self.offspring = self.sigma * (1.0 - e / ctx.epochs)

        idx = ctx.rng.integers(0, pop.size, pop.size)
        kids = parents[idx]
        noise = ctx.rng.standard_normal(kids.shape)

        mutated = self.mutate(
            kids, noise, self.offspring, ctx.bounds.low, ctx.bounds.up
        )

        n_pop = cm.PopulationSwarm(ctx.buff.snapshot)
        n_pop.compute << mutated

        mask = cm.is_best((n_pop.F, pop.F), ctx.sense)
        pop.assign[mask] << n_pop.access[mask]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    model = EvolutionStrategy(seed=42)

    def sphere(x):
        return float(np.sum(x**2))

    best_fitness, best_x = model.solve(
        sphere, cm.Bounds([(-1, 1)] * 5), epochs=100, pop_size=30
    )
    print("best fitness:", best_fitness)
    print("best solution:", best_x)

docs.title: Contract
docs.text:
Signature marker for reduce, e.g. Contract[[...], out].

Each input/output is a cast spec (Array / Scalar) or a plain dtype. A plain dtype is shorthand for Array[dtype, "n"]; ... is a scalar of default float dtype. Array[dtype] is a whole-array argument with a private dimension, and Array[dtype, "m,n"] names its dimensions::

Contract[[float, float, ..., ..., ...], float]          # (n),(n),(),(),()->(n)
Contract[[float, Array[float]], float]                   # (n),(k)->(n)
Contract[[Array[float, "m,n"], Array[float, "n,k"]],
         Array[float, "m,k"]]                            # (m,n),(n,k)->(m,k)

docs.title: precompile
docs.text:
precompile(*args: Any, fastmath: bool = False, parallel: bool = False, **kwargs: Any) -> typing.Any

Precompile a static method with numba.njit.

Specs can be passed positionally (cm.Array, cm.Array[float, 2]) or declared as annotations in the decorated function::

@cm.precompile
def hunt(X: "Array[float, 2]", a: "Scalar[float]"): ...

fastmath and parallel map to the numba.njit options of the same name (parallel also needs numba.prange in the body). A model can also enable them for every kernel at instantiation. Any other numba option (cache=True, boundscheck=False, ...) is forwarded through keyword arguments.

docs.title: vectorize
docs.text:
vectorize(*args: Any, fastmath: bool = False, parallel: bool = False, **kwargs: Any) -> typing.Any

Vectorize a static method, optionally precompiling it.

Specs can be passed positionally (cm.Array, cm.Scalar[float, [...]]) or declared as annotations in the decorated function::

@cm.vectorize
def affine(r: "Scalar[float]", a: "Scalar[float]") -> "Scalar[float]": ...

Precompilation needs a full signature because numba requires the return type. fastmath and parallel can be forced on the kernel, and a model can also provide them for every kernel at instantiation. Any other option is forwarded as a keyword.

docs.title: reduce
docs.text:
reduce(signatures: Any = None, layout: str | None = None, *, fastmath: bool = False, parallel: bool = False, **kwargs: Any) -> typing.Any

Build a generalized ufunc (numba.guvectorize) static method.

Three additive forms are supported:

  • Legacy numba style: a list of core type specs plus a layout, e.g. [cm.Array[float, 1], cm.Scalar[float], cm.Array[float, 1]] with "(n),()->(n)".

  • The Contract marker, which encodes the core types and layout::

    @cm.reduce(Contract[[Array[float, "m,n"], Array[float, "n,k"]], Array[float, "m,k"]]) def matmul(a, b, out): ...

  • Fully typed annotations, with the layout inferred (the last parameter is the output)::

    @cm.reduce def matmul(a: "Array[float, 'm,n']", b: "Array[float, 'n,k']", out: "Array[float, 'm,k']"): ...

fastmath maps to the numba option and parallel sets target="parallel"; any other option is forwarded as a keyword. A model can also provide fastmath/parallel/cache at instantiation.

docs.text:
apply(x: NDArrayType, idx: int | slice | list[int] | None = None) -> None

Vectorizes the target function to evaluate and update the solutions matrix.

Turn a class into a model (the class-style API).

docs.title: Argument
docs.text:
Declare a tunable, range-checked model field.

Argument is a subscript-only marker that builds a typing.Annotated type understood by @cm.declare / @cm.template. It is never instantiated — only subscripted on a class annotation. Supported forms::

Argument[type]                  # required, no range/default
Argument[type, default]         # with a default value
Argument[type, (min, max)]      # range-checked, required
Argument[type, (min, max), default]

The subscript accepts target_type (the field's type), optionally a (min_val, max_val) range, and optionally a default_val. An unsupported form raises TypeError.

docs.title: Variable
docs.text:
Declare a free internal-state field (no range check, no default).

Variable is a subscript-only marker for model state that is not a tunable parameter::

w: cm.Variable[np.ndarray]

It wraps target_type (the field's declared type) in typing.Annotated metadata marking it as delayed-init state.

TargetFunction(target: Target, bounds: Bounds, max_nfe: Optional[int] = None)

Wraps an objective, counting NFE and enforcing an optional budget.

The wrapper scores solutions row-by-row (or whole-block via evaluate_matrix for vectorized targets), increments the function-evaluation counter on every call, and raises MaxNumberOfCalls once max_nfe is spent.

docs.title: VectorizedTarget
docs.text:
VectorizedTarget(target: Target)

A target that maps a whole (pop, ndim) matrix to a (pop,) vector.

Marking a target as vectorized lets KernelBuffer.apply score a whole population with a single call instead of np.apply_along_axis, which spends one Python call per individual.

docs.title: vectorized_target
docs.text:
vectorized_target(target: Target) -> VectorizedTarget

Declare target as able to evaluate a whole (pop, ndim) block.

The wrapped callable receives a 2-D array and must return one value per row, so np.sum(x**2, axis=1) replaces a per-row comprehension. The result is identical to the row-by-row evaluation, only dispatched once.

Examples:

::

def sphere(x):           # x: (pop, ndim) -> (pop,)
    return np.sum(x**2, axis=1)

model.solve(cm.vectorized_target(sphere), bounds, 100, 40)
